plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two orbital drawings of a carbon-carbon double bond separated by a labeled arrow, before and after a twist. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" are stacked diagonally, each drawn with a pink lobe above and a blue lobe below, the lobes tapering to points at the carbon and each pink lobe carrying a small black dot. The two sets are parallel, and thin straight lines run along the outer edges of the upper pink pair and the lower blue pair to show that the lobes line up so their broad faces overlap sideways; short black bars and dashed lines at each carbon mark the remaining bonds and the plane they occupy. A horizontal arrow across the middle is labeled "rotate 90°". On the right the lower carbon is unchanged, but the upper one has been turned so its pink lobe points toward the viewer at the left and its blue lobe away at the right, leaving the two pairs crossing at right angles instead of running parallel. Bold labels beneath read "π bond (p orbitals are parallel)" and "Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)". Setting the aligned lobes against the crossed ones makes sideways overlap the thing to watch, explaining why twisting such a bond costs the full strength of the pi bond and so does not happen freely.

small black electron dot inside each pink/red lobe

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a single transformable version of the textbook’s two panels rather than showing both panels at once. World scale: lower C at approximately (0, 0, 0), upper C at approximately (1.8, 1.35, 0), joined by a thin black sigma-bond line. The C-C bond axis is the rotation axis for the upper carbon/orbital. Lower p orbital is fixed, centered on lower C, with local orbital axis about 15 degrees left of vertical in screen space: approximately direction (-0.25, 0.97, 0). Each lobe length about 1.05 units from carbon to rounded end, maximum radius about 0.45 units, pinched to nearly zero at the carbon. Upper p orbital has the same size; at 0 degrees its axis is parallel to the lower p orbital, and at 90 degrees it is rotated about the C-C bond so the red lobe swings toward the viewer/left and the blue lobe swings away/right, visually matching the source’s crossed-orbital panel. Use Rodrigues rotation about the normalized C-C axis for intermediate slider values. Positive-phase lobes are glossy pink/red #e94f78 with highlights #ff9aae; negative-phase lobes are glossy blue #2f86c7 with highlights #8dccf2. Electron dots are small black spheres, radius about 0.045 units, placed inside the pink lobes roughly 55% of the way from carbon to lobe tip. Carbon labels are black serif or textbook-style sans text, size about 0.18 world units, slightly offset in front of the orbital pinch point so they remain readable. Lower substituent bond stubs: two short thick black cylinders/lines length 0.45 units from lower C, one down-left and one down-right. Upper planar guide/stub lines: thin dashed black segments extending from upper C roughly left/up-left and right/up-right in the aligned state; fade or rotate with the upper carbon as dashed construction lines. Aligned-overlap guide lines are thin black lines running along the outer boundaries of the paired upper pink lobes and paired lower blue lobes, parallel to the p axes; show strongly near 0 degrees and fade out by about 45 degrees. At 90 degrees, show dashed perpendicular guide lines near the upper carbon. π-bond strength should be max(0, cos(theta)) where theta is the rotation angle in radians; map this to a horizontal bar from 0 to 1 under or beside the figure. Caption text should switch or interpolate: at 0 degrees, 'π bond (p orbitals are parallel)'; at 90 degrees, 'Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)'.
interactionPlan.notes: Render orbitals as smooth translucent/glossy implicit surfaces, metaballs, or custom lathed teardrop meshes with tapered tips at each carbon. Keep the carbon labels and electron dots billboarded or slightly depth-biased so they are not hidden by translucent lobes. The toggle should snap the rotationAngle slider to 0 or 90 degrees; moving the slider manually should update the orbitalState visually without requiring a third toggle option. Use alpha blending carefully: draw blue/red lobes with depth sorting or weighted transparency so overlapping p orbitals remain legible. Keep the view close to the source figure: diagonal C-C framework rising left-to-right, lower p orbital upright, upper p orbital initially parallel, and no perspective convergence emphasized.

authoredContext:
Although essentially free rotation around single bonds is possible (another section), the same is not true of double bonds. For rotation to occur around a double bond, the π bond must break and re-form (the figure). Thus, the barrier to double-bond rotation must be at least as great as the strength of the π bond itself, an estimated 350 kJ/mol (84 kcal/mol). Recall that the barrier to bond rotation in ethane is only 12 kJ/mol.

The π bond must break for rotation to take place around a carbon–carbon double bond.

An orbital diagram with two parallel p orbitals before rotation. After rotation the p orbitals are perpendicular, which breaks the double bond.

The lack of rotation around carbon–carbon double bonds is of more than just theoretical interest; it also has chemical consequences. Imagine the situation for a disubstituted alkene such as 2-butene. (Disubstituted means that two substituents other than hydrogen are bonded to the double-bond carbons.) The two methyl groups in 2-butene can either be on the same side of the double bond or on opposite sides, a situation similar to that in disubstituted cycloalkanes (another section).

plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two orbital drawings of a carbon-carbon double bond separated by a labeled arrow, before and after a twist. On the left, two carbons lettered "C" are stacked diagonally, each drawn with a pink lobe above and a blue lobe below, the lobes tapering to points at the carbon and each pink lobe carrying a small black dot. The two sets are parallel, and thin straight lines run along the outer edges of the upper pink pair and the lower blue pair to show that the lobes line up so their broad faces overlap sideways; short black bars and dashed lines at each carbon mark the remaining bonds and the plane they occupy. A horizontal arrow across the middle is labeled "rotate 90°". On the right the lower carbon is unchanged, but the upper one has been turned so its pink lobe points toward the viewer at the left and its blue lobe away at the right, leaving the two pairs crossing at right angles instead of running parallel. Bold labels beneath read "π bond (p orbitals are parallel)" and "Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)". Setting the aligned lobes against the crossed ones makes sideways overlap the thing to watch, explaining why twisting such a bond costs the full strength of the pi bond and so does not happen freely.

demo_steps.title: Parallel p orbitals: π bond present
demo_steps.narration: Both p orbitals face the same way, so the pink lobes overlap side-by-side and the blue lobes overlap side-by-side. The π-bond-strength bar is full.

demo_steps.title: Partial twist weakens overlap
demo_steps.narration: As the upper carbon rotates, its p orbital no longer lines up face-to-face with the lower one. The overlap indicator falls according to the cosine of the twist angle.

demo_steps.title: Perpendicular p orbitals: π bond broken
demo_steps.narration: At 90 degrees the upper p orbital is perpendicular to the lower p orbital. Their sideways overlap is zero, so the π bond has been broken.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use a single transformable version of the textbook’s two panels rather than showing both panels at once. World scale: lower C at approximately (0, 0, 0), upper C at approximately (1.8, 1.35, 0), joined by a thin black sigma-bond line. The C-C bond axis is the rotation axis for the upper carbon/orbital. Lower p orbital is fixed, centered on lower C, with local orbital axis about 15 degrees left of vertical in screen space: approximately direction (-0.25, 0.97, 0). Each lobe length about 1.05 units from carbon to rounded end, maximum radius about 0.45 units, pinched to nearly zero at the carbon. Upper p orbital has the same size; at 0 degrees its axis is parallel to the lower p orbital, and at 90 degrees it is rotated about the C-C bond so the red lobe swings toward the viewer/left and the blue lobe swings away/right, visually matching the source’s crossed-orbital panel. Use Rodrigues rotation about the normalized C-C axis for intermediate slider values. Positive-phase lobes are glossy pink/red #e94f78 with highlights #ff9aae; negative-phase lobes are glossy blue #2f86c7 with highlights #8dccf2. Electron dots are small black spheres, radius about 0.045 units, placed inside the pink lobes roughly 55% of the way from carbon to lobe tip. Carbon labels are black serif or textbook-style sans text, size about 0.18 world units, slightly offset in front of the orbital pinch point so they remain readable. Lower substituent bond stubs: two short thick black cylinders/lines length 0.45 units from lower C, one down-left and one down-right. Upper planar guide/stub lines: thin dashed black segments extending from upper C roughly left/up-left and right/up-right in the aligned state; fade or rotate with the upper carbon as dashed construction lines. Aligned-overlap guide lines are thin black lines running along the outer boundaries of the paired upper pink lobes and paired lower blue lobes, parallel to the p axes; show strongly near 0 degrees and fade out by about 45 degrees. At 90 degrees, show dashed perpendicular guide lines near the upper carbon. π-bond strength should be max(0, cos(theta)) where theta is the rotation angle in radians; map this to a horizontal bar from 0 to 1 under or beside the figure. Caption text should switch or interpolate: at 0 degrees, 'π bond (p orbitals are parallel)'; at 90 degrees, 'Broken π bond after rotation (p orbitals are perpendicular)'.
interactionPlan.notes: Render orbitals as smooth translucent/glossy implicit surfaces, metaballs, or custom lathed teardrop meshes with tapered tips at each carbon. Keep the carbon labels and electron dots billboarded or slightly depth-biased so they are not hidden by translucent lobes. The toggle should snap the rotationAngle slider to 0 or 90 degrees; moving the slider manually should update the orbitalState visually without requiring a third toggle option. Use alpha blending carefully: draw blue/red lobes with depth sorting or weighted transparency so overlapping p orbitals remain legible. Keep the view close to the source figure: diagonal C-C framework rising left-to-right, lower p orbital upright, upper p orbital initially parallel, and no perspective convergence emphasized.
